rv.q: It’s sharp, stylish, consistently compelling and effortlessly entertaining.
The result is a bracing, provocative and scintillatingly written drama that, as with her breakout play 1536, revisits the past to offer a scathing portrait of the world today.
Ava Pickett’s superb new play is a rip-roaring dark comedy set in the aftermath of a British Trojan War.
Spirling got the script for Bloodsport when she was running Theatre503 and it’s turned into a coup for her new berth as artistic director of Stratford East.
What comes next is a truly tense two hours.
It is flawed, unfocused and overburdened with the posturing of youth – but it also brims with an energy that is as wild as it is irresistible.
In its present form the tension seeps away in the second half.
The tension and cleverness of its conception never falters, and the words rise like a sword taking on the world.
Bloodsport is a shrewd analysis of how hatred grows, and the parts of society it ostracises.
Cee (Laura Aikman) has settled into the life of an Essex Princess with her husband Mario (Gerard Monaco).
For all its flaws, Bloodsport: After Helen of Troy remains compelling theatre.
For all that, the text is ripe, ribald and energised.
This is a play that centres on women having agency and includes a very entertaining narrator, but the interesting dialogue and shades of gangster plot lack a focus and have a puzzling conclusion.
The reality is that it’s as splashy as it is shallow.
It’s a compelling idea, but the execution often feels more like an episode of EastEnders and not one of the better ones.
Director Lisa Spirling emphasises the claustrophobia and the chaos contained within the house perfectly, as does Nicola T. Chang’s thumping and bolshy soundtrack.

Ava Pickett is an embodiment of the Jane Austen dictum that you should write about what you know. And what Pickett knows (her true worldview is of course cosmopolitan and urbane) is Essex. So it should be no surprise that she sets the aftermath of the Trojan Wars on the county’s approximation to a sunshine coast.

Ava Pickett is an incredibly gifted writer, and there are moments where her talent shines through, though it isn’t always clear to see in Bloodsport. There are many laugh-out-loud moments where Pickett’s witty writing thrills, but it proves less successful in its attempt to convey the serious message at the heart of the story.

Marcus and his friend Mario (married to Cee) go after Paris and bring Helen home – with no thought given to whether she actually wants to be rescued. What follows is a decade-long civil conflict: riots, looting, petrol bombs, foreigners dragged from hotels and their businesses burned, all justified by the idea that Helen is worthy of saving.

Bloodsport is immediately funny, although it's definitely not a comedy. There were many barbed retorts drawing guffaws from the audience. There's violence on and off set, but despite the early consideration of delicate furnishings and clothing, it never goes full-on Tarantino.

cn.t: Pickett's provocative Essex-set reimagining of Helen of Troy divides critics with its bold feminist fury and dark humor. Most praise the scintillating writing and Dockery's performance, though some find it unfocused and overwrought.
